title: How Invokyr sold ~250k copies with... Jumanji horror cool?
author: Simon Carless
excerpt: Also: this week on Steam & a bunch of discovery news.
text:
How Invokyr sold ~250k copies with... Jumanji horror cool?
Also: this week on Steam & a bunch of discovery news.
Simon Carless
10 hours ago
∙ Paid
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
Hey all - as we all take stock of the 7,000+ demos (!) in Steam Next Fest, we did a LinkedIn analysis discussing the AI disclosure percentage : 2,498 out of the 7,217 demos in total (34.6%.) That’s up from 21.2% of games in Feb's Next Fest and 26.5% in June's. (We’ll have larger-picture analysis this coming Tuesday, as we mentioned.)
After picking 5 random AI disclosures, they cluster around things like store page icons & placeholder localization. (We wouldn’t call these 100% ‘AI first’ games.) But as we add: “ First, AI code helper use doesn't have to be disclosed.. and second, people may deliberately only disclose smaller things.” So it’s confusing: Schrodinger’s slop ?
Before we start, maybe some nostalgic photos at this trying time? Great: the Video Game History Foundation just launched the Colin Williamson photography collection , “from a game journalist who was embedded in Japan from 1999 through the mid-2000s” , including TGS, Space World, and Akihabara pics from a golden age.
[ NEED THE BEST DATA? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP server, by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Basic gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more.]
Game disco news: most-played games of 2026…
Let’s finish the week with another chunk of game platform & discovery news:
We pulled an updated list of biggest median playtime Steam games in 2026 with >100k players from GDCo Pro & besides desktop idlers taking the top spots, Slay The Spire 2 is still a monster (52 hours, ~8m players!) , w/newer entries including the latest NBA 2K & EA Sports FCs, plus Forza 6 and (impressively!) Wardogs.
A new Fortune report on Xbox , filtered via VGC , includes plans for a “next-generation handheld device” by holiday 2027 and console by 2028, says: “As it stands, the price of the Helix console has internally been projected to cost consumers between $1,200 and $1,800… unless Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost.” That’s… non-cheap.
Max Power Gaming took a look at the Roblox charts for September , and it’s that egg-stealin’ game again: “After finishing second behind Murder Mystery 2 in August, Steal an Egg surged to an average of 1.4 million concurrent players, more than three times the audience of its nearest challenger, Brookhaven.”
The folks at super-popular YouTube analysis channel Bellular News took on the Steam Daily/Weekend Sale redesign , and this very missive is described as “an excellent newsletter” , as they agreed with us that removing ‘friction’ over how well devs know Valve with algorithms could actually work - if the algorithms gel.
Xbox things: Xbox Insiders get to try ‘a la carte’ Xbox cloud playtime , which is 10 hrs for $4, 25 for $8, and 50 for $12; new Game Pass titles include Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade, The Séance of Blake Manor & more ; the new Xbox Labs folks have been showing off (emulated?) oldskool Xbox bootup sequences on X.
A Steam change spotted by our GDCo Basic/Pro Discord crew: you now have to tag at least 5 screenshots with ‘gameplay’ before launching your Steam page, and at least one video, too. (Steam always had a similar rule , and would reject if not, but didn’t set up their UI to explicitly have you tag/agree before submitting.)
The consulting firm Vivrato have been surveying game execs about their firms’ usage of AI , noting: “94% use AI in at least one of nine production stages, but 52% rate how deeply it is built into their full production pipeline at three or lower out of 10.” (This ‘wider but shallow’ integration makes sense - there’s some posturing going on.)
GameDiscoverCo took a quick look at most-watched unreleased games on Twitch in the last 7 days , and it's striking to see the relative lack of Steam Next Fest titles (so far!) Valve's perpetually in-beta 6 vs. 6 MOBA/shooter Deadlock is #1, and alt-history Napoleonic extraction RPG Hunger (watch this game!) is coming in hot at #2. ( ‘Next Fest x Twitch’ winners? ArcheAge Chronicles, Find The Needle, Loftia…)
Xbox things, Pt. 2: AMD’s FSR 4.1 for image sharpening - similar to Sony’s QSSR - is due on Xbox Series X & S shortly ; Microsoft is reportedly sending e-mails to lapsed Xbox console users to sell their consoles to Best Buy; the IGN x ID@Xbox streaming showcase included a co-op hole digging game & Arctic Eggs → Xbox.
Well, that PHP vulnerability was a bit of a fire drill, huh? Among a host of websites, PC game platforms were seemingly taken down to patch, with a Steam downtime on Wednesday likely (?) linked to a fix, and GOG taken down for around four hours to remediate. Fun.
Microlinks: Nvidia’s DLSS AI detail tech is coming to Hogwarts Legacy & Where Winds Meet ; ; Google is adding a Game Finder discovery mechanism to Google Play; top ‘trad media’ mentions for the week inc. GTA VI, CoD: Modern Warfare 4, and Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (re: the remake.)
OUR SPONSOR: IsThereAnyDeal - video game market tracker
Looking for a way to track prices, bundles, and vouchers from legitimate PC stores for your games across several regions? IsThereAnyDeal has you covered!
IsThereAnyDeal is a convenient toolbox to check that shops are following your pricing strategy, track competitors, and research trends utilizing our detailed price history.
If you’re an indie dev, reach out to get your games featured on our front page Spotlight. (And if you’re a player as well, get notified about sales with your own customized price alerts!)
How Invokyr sold ~250k copies w/Jumanji cool?
It’s been a busy October for new Steam/console releases. But when looking for a game to highlight, we looked at ‘Oct. releases with the highest Steam concurrents’ . And lo and behold, among much bigger titles like Star Wars Galactic Racer, we spotted Ludogram’s “co-op survival horror game about a cursed board game” Invokyr in the top 10.
This $13 (launch discounted to $9.74) title launched on Oct. 8th, and we’re estimating it at ~250,000 copies sold, perhaps a ~$2m gross, and topped out at ~10,000 Steam concurrents. Its CCU chart is impressively scaled/stable - and atypically spiky, partly due to China (co-published via Shochiku) being ~48% of players, according to the devs:
So while this may not yet be a $25m-grossing smash just due to its lower cost of entry, we’d def. expect it to hit $5-$10m on Steam over time. And in today’s crowded market, that’s a great result. So we talked to Ludogram’s Edouard Gaudel (CEO/creative director) and César Grislain (game director) - here’s some of our takeaway on why:
The game mashes up horror, randomness, and cursed board games so well: go look at the RDC Gaming crew playing Invokyr ~100% incoherently - tell us it’s not fun to watch? Ludogram tells us they started with the idea of a RPG with an interfering GM, before getting inspired by actual ‘90s horror TV board game Nightmare/Atmosfear . (And later removing the VHS/TV element altogether…)
The ‘creepy Jumanji’ board game hook is incredibly robust: it can’t be overstated how much a natural YouTuber & player comp to another popular thing can help your virality. And in this case, ‘it’s like Jumanji - the original movie’ 100% works. A lot of Steam player reviews mention it too, even tho it’s not in the marketing.
There’s more roguelite in here than many similar titles: having a central hub board game & a) rolling to advance levels & get random quests/bad guys, and b) finding in-level dice with weird good/bad effects - differentiates it from other co-op. Ludogram’s other teams working on Monsters Are Coming & Ascenders both use roguelite mechanics, so they “are often part of our broader design culture.”
Invokyr didn’t have a particular large dev team, btw, but also not a tiny one, spanning between 6 and 12 devs during ~two years of development. What they’ve managed to pull off has good fidelity at ‘above-tiny dev’ levels. (Side note: surely somebody will be tempted to license a movie adaptation of this concept?)
We also wanted to talk about the fact that Invokyr’s gameplay feels really well-polished at launch. Well - it is, and that’s because Ludogram did a ton(ne) of iteration. According to what Edouard & César told us re: the playtest process:
“Playtests & demos were a really important part of the creation process for Invokyr. The first playtest was in September 2025. Feedback was good, but we had issues with players not focusing on the board aspect of the game. We did 2nd & 3rd [smaller] playtests in February and April 2026, then a demo released in May, updated in July, a closed beta in September 2026.”
Maybe it’s getting a little tiring for some of you to see co-op and horror games take off yet again. But look - with Phasmophobia at 25 million copies sold as of July 2025 ( we have 53% of Invokyr players as also owning Phasmophobia) , there’s plenty of juice still out there for this type of title. (Maybe proficient takes on co-op horror are under-served?)
And proficiency is key - look at GDCo Pro Steam player review data for Invokyr. It’s pretty rare to see almost no red/negative bars in our review sentiment topics:
Some final notes: a) the Invokyr demo topped out at ~2,000 CCU, so there was some indication the full game was going to do well b) we estimate (a v.good!) 3 hours and 48 minutes median playtime so far, and we’d expect that to stretch up. c) Twitch activity is also jumpin’ - #67 from the 28,800 games we tracked in the last 7 days.
This week on Steam: CoD, FF Resonance, more…

title: Version 7: Bringing Market Research Into The Games We Make
author: Ross Burton, PhD
text:
Version 7: Bringing Market Research Into The Games We Make
Share:
Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Devlogs
Published: 10/23/2026
Updated: 10/23/2026
We started Game Oracle as a market research platform. The objective was pretty simple: we wanted to understand the Steam market, find relevant competitors, explore opportunities and make better decisions about the games we wanted to build.
But as we thought about what we needed for our own games, we kept coming back to the same nagging problem. You see finding useful information is only part of the work. You still have to turn it into a design, a plan, and something you can actually make.
There is so much to be gained by the data out there. A competitor's reviews might change how you approach progression or difficulty, a group of games might challenge your assumptions about price, and something as simple as a screenshot might help you explain the atmosphere you're trying to create. All of these discoveries need somewhere to go, and they need to stay useful as the game takes shape.
That's the thinking behind v7 of Game Oracle. We want the research you do to inform your planning and design, and we want you to be able to return to that data whenever development raises a new question.
A Concept Compass report becomes an editable project: a draft GDD, vision board and competitor radar, with the Scrapbook research alongside. Give your research somewhere to live
The first piece of our new and improved experience is the Scrapbook .
As you explore Game Oracle, you can collect research into a project: games, images, colour palettes, useful passages, statistics, charts, saved searches and tables of games. You can add notes so you remember what caught your attention and why it matters.
That last part is all too easy for us to underestimate. Saving a reference is useful yes, but remembering what you wanted to learn from it is much more useful. Was it the way the game introduces its systems? The readability of its art? Something players repeatedly praised or complained about? I've personally been noting all the ways players complain about balancing difficulty since it is something I seem to struggle with most!
Scrapbook gives all these discoveries a home. You can return to a saved search, revisit the source of a statistic or bring a reference into the work you're doing next.
The Workspace is then where that next step happens. Each project has a place for documents, whiteboards, competitor research, data comparisons and workboards. The research you've collected stays within reach while you write, sketch, and plan. It will also form the basis of data-driven tools that we plan to keep rolling out. We want to make it incredibly easy to inform your decisions with market data from competitors similar to your concept.
From "could this idea work?" to a starting point
Concept Compass already helps you investigate an idea: describe the game, choose its defining features and inspirations, then explore comparable games, player sentiment, projections, and practical considerations.
For us, validation means using that evidence to test assumptions. Which games share the experience we're trying to create? What do their players value? Where might our scope or expectations need another look?
However, starting from v7 that research can now become the starting point for your project. Simply choose Add to Project on a completed concept and Game Oracle populates its Workspace with:
A Draft GDD you can edit and develop.
A Project Vision whiteboard covering the pitch, audience, experience and design pillars.
A Competitor Radar containing competitors from the report.
A Research Board bringing together findings, projections, resources and marketing ideas.
A Concept Report item so you can revisit the analysis.
Capsule Art Analysis , when the concept has competitors, to help explore visual direction.
You can start working on items as they appear. The generated material gives you something concrete to question, rearrange, and make your own.
Keeping all your evidence next to your design
This is the part we're especially interested in for our own games. We want to be able to work on a vision with the research right there beside it.
In a Workspace document, you can write your GDD, pitch or development notes and bring in material from Scrapbook. Drop in a table of comparable games, a saved chart, a statistic linked to its source, or an annotated image. A research snippet can sit beside the design decision it helped you make.
Imagine writing a section about level progression. You could put actual relevant player feedback beside your proposed approach, then explain what you want to test in the prototype. When you revisit that section later, the reasoning is still there.
Whiteboards give you even more room to explore the same material but visually. You can map out a core loop, arrange references into a mood board, sketch a level, or build a positioning map. The flexible design makes it easy to bring in images, palettes, research cards, and charts, then add your own connections and questions around them.
And when an idea is ready to become work, a Workboard can hold the stories and tasks, with links back to Workspace pages or Scrapbook clippings. All of this means that the reason for building something can travel with the task and can be constantly cross-checked for relevance. Personally, we think this is a game changer for scope creep!
Keep the evidence beside the design: player feedback and feature research from the Scrapbook, pinned next to the project's production notes on a Research Board. Ask the question your game actually needs
As a game or concept becomes more specific, the questions tend to become more specific too. We found that the current search tools in Game Oracle were not quite up-to-scratch for this.
A broad genre overview might help at the start, but later you might want to look only at paid indie games released in a particular period, with certain mechanics, a demo, and enough reviews to make the comparison useful. Or you might want to ask a question about the exact shortlist you've already collected for your project.
Powersearch lets you go further into those questions. You can write SQL against the available Steam catalogue data, or describe what you're looking for in plain English and generate a query to review and run.
For example:
“Find paid indie roguelikes released from 2023 to 2025 that have a demo, at least 50 reviews and at least 80% positive reviews.”
“Within my saved shortlist, what is the median estimated Steam revenue for each game engine?”
“Among games with a particular mechanic, how do review scores vary across launch-price bands?”
Queries that return games can feed straight back into Data Explorer's tables and charts. You can also save those games as a dataset, and use a saved dataset to limit a later query.
All of this makes research much more iterative. You start with a question, inspect the results, refine the group, and then ask the next question, all whilst keeping an audit trial of your data in your scrapbook.
Ask a specific question, inspect the SQL and run it against Game Oracle's Steam data. Compare alternative data and build confidence
Now that we have a way of crafting and saving specific datasets we also wanted to give users a way of comparing subsets of games. This is especially useful if you're stuck between one concept or another.
Data Comparisons lets you put two saved datasets or competitor sets side by side. The tables, charts, and descriptive statistics help you examine how those groups differ, with shared chart scales so the comparison stays readable.
You can compare typical values using medians and an uncertainty interval, rather than letting one unusually successful game dominate your impression. You can also compare player-review summaries to explore the praise and complaints that appear more often in each group.
Say you're considering two approaches to a visual style. You could build a set of relevant games for each, compare their market data, then look at what players say about them. The choice of games still matters, and a difference between groups doesn't establish what caused it. But it gives you a much more focused basis for the next design discussion or prototype.
For us, the exciting part is having that whole process connected. You define a precise group in Powersearch, compare it with another group, save the useful evidence, and bring it into the document or board where you're working through the decision.
Research that stays part of development
We built v7 because we wanted market research to keep helping us after we'd chosen an idea.
As we build, we'll have new questions about features, art direction, positioning, and scope. We want to explore those questions without losing the connection between what we've learned and what we're making.
Scrapbook, Workspace and the deeper research tools are our next step towards that. It means we can collect what matters, use it to shape our game, and come back to the evidence as our thinking changes.
If you already have a completed concept, try adding it to a project and developing one part of the generated vision. If you're still exploring, start by collecting a few references and see what sort of questions they raise.
We'd love to hear which decisions you're trying to make about your game, and what would help you make them with more confidence.

  • A Concept Report item so you can revisit the analysis.
  • Capsule Art Analysis, when the concept has competitors, to help explore visual direction.

You can start working on items as they appear. The generated material gives you something concrete to question, rearrange, and make your own.

Keeping all your evidence next to your design

This is the part we're especially interested in for our own games. We want to be able to work on a vision with the research right there beside it.

In a Workspace document, you can write your GDD, pitch or development notes and bring in material from Scrapbook. Drop in a table of comparable games, a saved chart, a statistic linked to its source, or an annotated image. A research snippet can sit beside the design decision it helped you make.

Imagine writing a section about level progression. You could put actual relevant player feedback beside your proposed approach, then explain what you want to test in the prototype. When you revisit that section later, the reasoning is still there.

Whiteboards give you even more room to explore the same material but visually. You can map out a core loop, arrange references into a mood board, sketch a level, or build a positioning map. The flexible design makes it easy to bring in images, palettes, research cards, and charts, then add your own connections and questions around them.

And when an idea is ready to become work, a Workboard can hold the stories and tasks, with links back to Workspace pages or Scrapbook clippings. All of this means that the reason for building something can travel with the task and can be constantly cross-checked for relevance. Personally, we think this is a game changer for scope creep!

Ask the question your game actually needs

As a game or concept becomes more specific, the questions tend to become more specific too. We found that the current search tools in Game Oracle were not quite up-to-scratch for this.

A broad genre overview might help at the start, but later you might want to look only at paid indie games released in a particular period, with certain mechanics, a demo, and enough reviews to make the comparison useful. Or you might want to ask a question about the exact shortlist you've already collected for your project.

Powersearch lets you go further into those questions. You can write SQL against the available Steam catalogue data, or describe what you're looking for in plain English and generate a query to review and run.

For example:

  • “Find paid indie roguelikes released from 2023 to 2025 that have a demo, at least 50 reviews and at least 80% positive reviews.”
  •  “Within my saved shortlist, what is the median estimated Steam revenue for each game engine?”
  • “Among games with a particular mechanic, how do review scores vary across launch-price bands?”

Queries that return games can feed straight back into Data Explorer's tables and charts. You can also save those games as a dataset, and use a saved dataset to limit a later query.

All of this makes research much more iterative. You start with a question, inspect the results, refine the group, and then ask the next question, all whilst keeping an audit trial of your data in your scrapbook.

Compare alternative data and build confidence

Now that we have a way of crafting and saving specific datasets we also wanted to give users a way of comparing subsets of games. This is especially useful if you're stuck between one concept or another.

Data Comparisons lets you put two saved datasets or competitor sets side by side. The tables, charts, and descriptive statistics help you examine how those groups differ, with shared chart scales so the comparison stays readable.

You can compare typical values using medians and an uncertainty interval, rather than letting one unusually successful game dominate your impression. You can also compare player-review summaries to explore the praise and complaints that appear more often in each group.

Say you're considering two approaches to a visual style. You could build a set of relevant games for each, compare their market data, then look at what players say about them. The choice of games still matters, and a difference between groups doesn't establish what caused it. But it gives you a much more focused basis for the next design discussion or prototype.

For us, the exciting part is having that whole process connected. You define a precise group in Powersearch, compare it with another group, save the useful evidence, and bring it into the document or board where you're working through the decision.

Research that stays part of development

We built v7 because we wanted market research to keep helping us after we'd chosen an idea.

As we build, we'll have new questions about features, art direction, positioning, and scope. We want to explore those questions without losing the connection between what we've learned and what we're making.

Scrapbook, Workspace and the deeper research tools are our next step towards that. It means we can collect what matters, use it to shape our game, and come back to the evidence as our thinking changes.

If you already have a completed concept, try adding it to a project and developing one part of the generated vision. If you're still exploring, start by collecting a few references and see what sort of questions they raise.

We'd love to hear which decisions you're trying to make about your game, and what would help you make them with more confidence.
